test.name: A premise-verification question names the fact sought, not a name-property test
test.description: Regression for #1394. The objective is Rosalind Hartwell's parents, but her recorded surname 'Hartwell' is unverified — it may be her maiden name or the married name taken from her husband Thomas Hartwell (quality:1 tree data). Verifying that premise is correct, but the question must be framed so every branch names the fact the objective needs — her maiden name — not a bare maiden-vs-married property test whose 'married' branch names no fact and leaves the objective where it began. Synthetic scenario — no PII. Must coexist with the #1471 confirm-or-refute framing (a different scenario/tag), which this test does not exercise.

input.user_message: I want to find Rosalind Hartwell's parents. Pick the first research question to investigate.

judge_context: The objective is Rosalind Hartwell's parents, but her recorded surname 'Hartwell' is unverified — it may be her birth (maiden) name or a married name taken from her husband. The first research question must verify that premise by NAMING the fact the objective needs — her maiden (birth) name — e.g. 'What was Rosalind Hartwell's maiden name?'. Every branch of that answer yields a fact: if 'Hartwell' is her birth surname, a birth or baptism record confirms it; if not, the marriage record supplies the maiden name.

A bare property test of the name — e.g. 'Was Hartwell her maiden or married name?', 'Was Hartwell the birth surname of Rosalind?', or 'Determine whether she acquired Hartwell through marriage' — is WRONG: its 'married' / 'no' branch names no fact and leaves the objective exactly where it began (issue #1394). What fails is that SHAPE — a yes/no, either/or, or 'whether' classification whose branch can name no fact — not the vocabulary. An OPEN question that asks for the value itself is CORRECT whether it says 'maiden name' or 'birth surname': 'What was the birth surname of Rosalind?' names the gating fact exactly as 'What was her maiden name?' does, and both PASS. Grade the CLASS, not one wording: a premise-verification question fails only when its answer merely confirms, denies, or classifies the recorded name without naming the gating value.

This is distinct from the #1471 confirm-or-refute framing, which tests a disputed identity assertion already on the tree ('do independent records confirm or refute that X and Y are the parents of Z?') and does name a fact. That framing is correct in its own disputed-parents scenario and is not what this test grades.
